objectives: Distinguish user mode from kernel mode.

slides.title: User mode vs kernel mode
slides.body:
x86-64 + ARM64 CPUs have privilege rings:
- **Ring 0 (kernel mode)**: full access to hardware, I/O, memory.
- **Ring 3 (user mode)**: restricted; no direct hardware access; trapped by hardware on disallowed ops.

User-mode code cannot:
- Execute privileged CPU instructions (LIDT, MOV CR3, INVLPG, etc.).
- Access kernel-only memory regions.
- Do I/O directly.

To do these things, user code makes a **system call** (syscall): an instruction that transfers control to the kernel at a predefined entry point, with the CPU privilege level switched to ring 0.

The kernel does the work, then returns to user mode. The user-mode caller sees a result; the kernel internals stay hidden behind the syscall ABI. This is the fundamental contract: 'apps can do anything that the kernel mediates'.

slides.title: Syscall hardware path, x86-64
slides.body:
On x86-64, the `syscall` instruction is the fast path. The pre-existing mechanism (`int 0x80`) is slower + only used for legacy.

`syscall` instruction:
1. CPU saves user-mode RIP (instruction pointer) + RFLAGS into MSRs.
2. CPU loads kernel-mode CS, SS, RIP from MSRs (set up by the kernel at boot).
3. Privilege level switches to ring 0.
4. Kernel code runs: dispatches based on RAX (syscall number), arguments in RDI/RSI/RDX/R10/R8/R9.
5. `sysret` instruction: restores user-mode CS, SS, RIP from MSRs.
6. Returns to user mode with result in RAX.

Cost: ~50-200ns on modern CPUs. Spectre/Meltdown mitigations made syscalls 2-3× slower (KPTI = Kernel Page Table Isolation flushes some TLB on every syscall). On Linux post-2018, `perf stat` shows syscalls at ~200-500ns each.

**Implications**: syscall-per-byte I/O is hopeless (a 1MB read with 1 syscall per byte = 200ms just in syscall overhead). Batch + buffer. `read(fd, buf, 4096)` reads 4KB in one syscall instead of 4096.

slides.title: io_uring: the modern syscall bypass
slides.body:
Linux 5.1+ added **io_uring**: a submission queue + completion queue, both shared between user and kernel via mmap'd memory. App submits I/O operations to the queue; kernel processes them in background; app polls the completion queue.

Result: NO syscall per I/O operation. Submitting 1000 reads = 1 syscall (or zero if using busy-polling mode). Especially valuable for storage-heavy workloads (Postgres on NVMe, fio benchmarks).

Real-world impact:
- Benchmark loads ~2× faster with io_uring vs epoll on NVMe-heavy workloads.
- Some allocators + databases now use io_uring directly: ScyllaDB, postgres+pg_io_uring, BoringSSL's QUIC stack.
- nginx + Envoy still mostly on epoll; io_uring adoption is gradual.

The pattern (shared-memory queues bypassing syscalls) is broader: DPDK for networking, SPDK for storage, RDMA. The cost of crossing the user/kernel boundary keeps motivating these designs.

question.question: Estimate syscall overhead for naive I/O
question.goal: Read a 1MB file using `read(fd, buf, 1)` (one byte at a time). Per-syscall cost 500ns.

steps.reveal: 0.5 seconds JUST in syscall overhead — before any actual I/O.

steps.prompt: Same with `read(fd, buf, 4096)` (one page at a time):

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Buffered I/O: }\sim 4000\times \text{ faster than byte-at-a-time}}$$ Syscall overhead is fixed per call. Larger buffers amortize it. Every modern I/O library buffers automatically; `stdio` in C, `BufferedReader` in Java, BufWriter in Rust.

question.question: io_uring's main benefit over epoll for high-IOPS workloads:
options: No syscall per I/O operation — submissions + completions go through shared-memory queues.
question.explanation: io_uring amortizes syscall overhead by batching: many I/O operations go through one syscall (or zero, in polling mode). epoll still requires one syscall per readiness-check; io_uring eliminates this. For NVMe-class IOPS (~1M+/sec), saving ~500ns × 1M = 500ms/sec of CPU just on syscall overhead is a real gain.

hints: What's the per-op overhead of epoll vs io_uring?
Shared-memory queues mean no kernel transition per op.
slides.workedSolution: epoll: 1 syscall per wait + 1 per ready check + 1 per actual I/O. io_uring: shared-memory submission + completion queues; many I/O ops per syscall (or zero with polling). For high-IOPS storage (NVMe at 1M IOPS), the syscall overhead saved is 500ms/sec of CPU.

question.question: Slow application despite fast disk
question.prompt: A teammate's data-loading benchmark gets 50MB/s read throughput on an NVMe SSD that benchmarks at 5GB/s. Their code uses `read(fd, buf, 1)`. Walk through the diagnosis + fix.
Explain in two or three sentences why kernel-bypass technologies (io_uring, DPDK, RDMA) all share a common architectural pattern.
question.rubric: Mentions that all of them move I/O submissions + completions to shared-memory queues read/written by both user + kernel; eliminates per-op syscall transitions; preserves kernel's role for control-plane (setup) but bypasses it for data-plane (per-op processing); the speedup over syscall-per-op is substantial at high op rates.
